title: The hidden years
hookLine: thirty years in Nazareth, a trade, a village, nothing written down
carry: most of his life was ordinary

cards: A biography keeps the graduation, the wedding, the big move. It skips the ten thousand Tuesdays: the dishes, the commute, the afternoon someone fixed a chair. The Gospels go further.
There's the birth. There's one story at twelve. Then the next time Jesus appears, Luke says he's about thirty.
About eighteen years without a single scene. Catholics have a name for that silence: the hidden life.

teach.b: What's known is very little. Luke gives two sentences. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them."
And: "Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men." Grace, your very first word, again. He grew, the way children grow.
Mark adds one clue, years later, when the people of Nazareth are offended by him: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" The Greek word is tekton: a builder, a craftsman in wood or stone.
So it's possible to guess at a life. A small village. A family trade, likely learned from Joseph.
Rough hands, customers who paid late, neighbors' weddings and funerals. Probably Joseph's death somewhere in there, since he disappears from the story.

But those are guesses; the Gospels are silent. Later writers couldn't stand the silence, and stories appeared of a boy Jesus making clay birds fly and doing flashy miracles. The Church never accepted them as scripture.
The real tradition kept the silence, and found something in it.

If Jesus is who Catholics believe he is, then God spent about thirty years, of a life tradition counts at about thirty-three, doing ordinary work in a village no one had heard of. Hidden, and not wasted.
A French hermit named Charles de Foucauld, now a saint, spent years trying to live just like that, and called it living Nazareth.

teach.h: MOST OF HIS LIFE WAS ORDINARY.

how: Catholics honor the hidden life of Jesus on the feast of the Holy Family, after Christmas, and on the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker, May 1; many religious communities take Nazareth as a model of prayerful ordinary work.

games.q: the Gospels jump from Jesus at twelve to Jesus at about thirty. what do they tell us about the years in between?

almost nothing: he went home, obeyed, and grew.

games.why: two sentences in Luke: he was subject to them, and he advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace. the rest is silence.

practice: Bring to mind the most ordinary task ahead of you today: washing a pan, folding a shirt, driving the same road. Picture doing it slowly and well, the way a craftsman planes a board, with no one watching.
If you pray, offer it to God before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Tekton. Mark's Greek word for Jesus's trade: a builder in wood or stone, perhaps taught by Joseph in Nazareth.
